text:
"RAG is dead" is the latest industry hyperbole that misses the technical point.

A colleague dropped this during a deep dive into agent architectures last week.
He was wrong about the death of the pillar, but right about the shift in strategy.
We're moving from "embed everything" to surgical precision.

Compare the architecture of Cursor with Claude Code.
Cursor relies on permanent embeddings so the agent maps your entire codebase.
It's fast and fluid, but it creates significant data noise and consumes tokens at a high rate.
Claude Code takes a different path using grep and glob.
It uses regex-based search to find exactly what's needed for the specific task.

There's no wasted effort embedding files you'll never query.
You get exact matches instead of semantic approximations.
In software engineering, an approximation is often just a bug waiting to happen.
Precision beats proximity when you're looking for a specific function signature.

RAG was born out of necessity to give LLMs context they didn't have.
The failure mode is assuming every retrieval task requires a vector database.
Embeddings lack inherent direction.
They're a blunt instrument for high-precision tasks like code navigation.

My stack follows the data type, not the trend.
I use grep and glob for specific navigation within the file system.
I use BM25 for keyword-heavy search requirements.
I only embed what actually requires semantic understanding, like sprawling documentation.

RAG isn't dead.
It's just finally being used correctly by engineers who value efficiency over easy abstractions.

How are you balancing exact matching against semantic search in your current retrieval pipeline?

#AIEngineering #RAG #LLMs #SoftwareArchitecture
idea_source: RAGs are dead — that's what a colleague said the other day. It stuck with me because RAG is one of the pillars of data engineering. But he was right, in a specific context. He was explaining how Cursor works vs Claude Code: Cursor uses permanent embeddings so the agent always knows where everything is, updated constantly as new code is generated. Fast, efficient. But pricey and creates noise in the data. Claude Code, on the other hand, uses grep and glob — regex-based search to find exactly what's needed. No wasted tokens embedding things you never query. Exact matches, not approximations. Approximations can mislead. The deeper insight: RAGs were born out of necessity — to give LLMs better context. But they lack direction. New tools fill the gaps where RAGs are inefficient and costly. Today I use grep and glob for specific code navigation, BM25 for keyword search, and I only embed what actually needs semantic search — large documentation, not everything. The question engineers should ask: what kind of data are you dealing with? That determines the tool. RAG is not dead. It's just finally being used correctly.
